article: Paper #1, Part 1: What Does It Mean for a Computer to 'See' a Picture?

agreed_changes.proposed_fix: "For a color image, it's actually three numbers per cell: one for red, one for green, one for blue (RGB) — the standard format for digital cameras and screens, though other encodings like grayscale or CMYK exist for different purposes. An 800 × 600 image is really an 800 × 600 × 3 grid of numbers."

Add after the seven challenges: "Everything else in this series is really an answer to one question: how do we get a model to recognize that these wildly different arrays of numbers are, in some meaningful sense, the same thing? That property has a name: **invariance**. A good classifier needs to be invariant to viewpoint, scale, deformation, and the rest — while still being sensitive enough to tell a dog from a wolf."
"It's a foundational text in deep learning — foundational enough that Ilya Sutskever put it on the reading list he gave John Carmack."

negotiated_changes.proposed_fix: "In a digital photo, this has already happened. (Some image formats, like vector graphics, work differently — but every photo you take or download is stored this way.) Every photo is stored as a grid."
